VIDEO.title: The Most IMPOSSIBLE Verse in the Gospels?! (Matthew 5:21-48)
VIDEO.series: The Gospel of Matthew Every Word (playlist of 58 videos)

hand: 'Perfect' isn't flawless. It's whole, mature, blameless.
SUMMARY: The teacher reads Matthew 5:21-48: six times Jesus says 'You have heard... but I say to you,' on anger, lust, divorce, oaths, retaliation and love for enemies, ending with 'you are to be perfect, as your heavenly Father is perfect' (5:48).
The thread is personal relationships: anger with a brother, an opponent at law, lust, divorce, oaths, generosity, loving everyone. Our relationships are how we bring God's kingdom on earth.
These are not new commands. As the new Moses, Jesus re-teaches the Torah from the heart, against the backdrop of the scribes and Pharisees (5:20).

Jesus puts a 'fence around the Torah,' a rabbinic way of teaching, but His fence is around the heart, where sin begins. The Talmud compares public humiliation to shedding blood; Jesus goes deeper, to anger.
'Perfect' echoes the Hebrew tamim: blameless, whole, mature (2 Samuel 22:31; Deuteronomy 18:13; Psalm 15:2). The Bible is looking for maturity, not flawlessness.

The lesson: God loves His enemies, sending sun and rain on the evil and the good, so in His kingdom we love our enemies too. Sons do what the Father does (John 5:19). Will you be tamim as your heavenly Father is tamim?
QUOTES: When Jesus said that you must be perfect as your heavenly Father is perfect, He wasn't intending to make you anxious or fearful.
The fence that Jesus is placing forces His people to deal with what is on the inside, what is in their heart, which is where sin originates.
The Bible is not looking for flawlessness; it's looking for maturity.
God loves His enemies; therefore in God's kingdom we should be like God and love our enemies.
Will you love your enemies? Will you be tamim the way your heavenly Father is tamim?

method.h: Read the six sayings in pairs
method.p: Each saying has two halves: 'You have heard' (what the Law said) and 'But I say to you' (where Jesus takes it). Look up each Old Testament text first, then ask the video's question: is Jesus replacing the Torah, or showing its heart?

LSB_QUOTES.text: But I say to you that everyone who is angry with his brother shall be guilty before the court
But I say to you, love your enemies and pray for those who persecute you,
for He causes His sun to rise on the evil and the good, and sends rain on the righteous and the unrighteous.
Therefore you are to be perfect, as your heavenly Father is perfect.

SIX.title: Murder and anger

right.text: But I say to you that everyone who is angry with his brother shall be guilty before the court; and whoever says to his brother, ‘Raca,’ shall be guilty before the Sanhedrin; and whoever says, ‘You fool,’ shall be guilty enough to go into the fiery hell.

lines.text: If you bear anger in your heart, you're already on the path toward murder, because murder usually begins in anger.

Then two practical scenes: leave your offering at the altar and 'first be reconciled to your brother' (5:24), and make friends quickly with your opponent at law (5:25). Reconciliation comes before worship.

SIX.note: Chrysostom: 'Do you see authority in perfection? ... Which among prophets ever spoke on this wise? ... None; but, Thus says the Lord' (Homilies on Matthew 16).

right.text: but I say to you that everyone who looks at a woman to lust for her has already committed adultery with her in his heart.

lines.text: The shift is from actions performed in front of others to what only God sees, the heart.

The tenth commandment already reached the heart: 'You shall not covet your neighbor's wife' (Exodus 20:17). Tearing out an eye and cutting off a hand (5:29-30) is a vivid way of saying: deal ruthlessly with what leads you to sin.

left.text: and he writes her a certificate of divorce and puts it in her hand and sends her out from his house,

right.text: but I say to you that everyone who divorces his wife, except for the reason of sexual immorality, makes her commit adultery; and whoever marries a divorced woman commits adultery.

lines.text: Avoid divorce: the video points to Deuteronomy 24:1 and Jeremiah 3:1.

Deuteronomy 24 regulates divorce rather than commands it. Later Jesus explains: 'Because of your hardness of heart Moses permitted you to divorce your wives; but from the beginning it has not been this way' (Matthew 19:8). Compare Malachi 2:16.

left.text: And you shall not swear falsely by My name, so as to profane the name of your God; I am Yahweh.

right.text: But I say to you, make no oath at all, either by heaven, for it is the throne of God,

lines.text: The video lists Leviticus 19:12 and Numbers 30:2 behind this saying.
'Let your statement be, ‘Yes, yes’ or ‘No, no’' (5:37). If your word is always true, you don't need an oath to prop it up. Jesus later exposes clever oath rules in Matthew 23:16-22.

SIX.title: An eye for an eye

left.text: eye for eye, tooth for tooth, hand for hand, foot for foot,

right.text: But I say to you, do not resist an evil person; but whoever slaps you on your right cheek, turn the other to him also.

lines.text: Forgiving others and being radically generous.

In the Law, 'eye for eye' guided judges and limited revenge to fit the harm (Exodus 21:23-25; Leviticus 24:20; Deuteronomy 19:21). Leviticus 19:18 already said, 'You shall not take vengeance.' Jesus asks for more than restraint: turn the cheek, give the garment, go the second mile.

SIX.note: Chrysostom on 5:39-41: 'Do you see the height of self-denial?' (Homilies on Matthew 18).

SIX.title: Love your enemies

left.text: You shall not take vengeance, and you shall not keep your anger against the sons of your people, but you shall love your neighbor as yourself; I am Yahweh.

right.text: But I say to you, love your enemies and pray for those who persecute you, so that you may be sons of your Father who is in heaven

lines.text: The video's focus. Jewish sentiment had become tribal: love of neighbor reached only 'the sons of your people' (Leviticus 19:18). They had forgotten that God is for the outcast, the sojourner, the orphan and the widow.

'Hate your enemy' is not a command in the Law. The same chapter says of the sojourner, 'you shall love him as yourself' (Leviticus 19:34), and Exodus tells Israel to return an enemy's stray ox (Exodus 23:4-5).

SIX.note: Chrysostom on this last step: 'Do you see how many steps He has ascended, and how He has set us on the very summit of virtue?' (Homilies on Matthew 18).

src.text: make a fence round the Torah

lines.text: Imagine sin as a place on a map. A fence keeps you far from it. Other rabbis did this, but Jesus' fence is not more outward rules that can be performed for others to see; it is around the heart.

This saying is credited to the Men of the Great Assembly at the start of the Mishnah's tractate Avot ('Fathers'), written down around AD 200. Translation: Joshua Kulp, Mishnah Yomit (CC BY), via Sefaria.

src.text: Anyone who humiliates another in public, it is as though he were spilling blood.

lines.text: The Talmud, the written account of the oral Torah, says this. Jesus goes further back, to anger in the heart. Public humiliation doesn't go deep enough; it doesn't track back to the source.

The Talmud was compiled centuries after Jesus (around AD 500). This saying is quoted there as an older teaching, so it may reflect earlier rabbis, but we cannot be sure it was taught in Jesus' day. Translation: William Davidson edition (CC BY-NC), via Sefaria.

left.text: Then they will go forth and look / On the corpses of the men / Who have transgressed against Me. / For their worm will not die / And their fire will not be quenched;

right.text: it is better for you to enter the kingdom of God with one eye, than, having two eyes, to be cast into hell, where their worm does not die, and the fire is not quenched.

lines.text: When Jesus speaks of hell or the judgment of fire (5:22, 29), He is drawing on Isaiah 66:15 to the end of the chapter. Read Isaiah 66 alongside Matthew 5:22-30.
Mark's version of the eye saying quotes Isaiah 66:24 outright. 'Hell' is Gehenna, the valley of the son of Hinnom outside Jerusalem, where children had been burned to idols (Jeremiah 7:31-32).

src.text: As for God, His way is blameless; / The word of Yahweh is tried; / He is a shield to all who take refuge in Him.

lines.text: The Hebrew word here is tamim: blameless. And Jesus says, be like this.

src.text: You shall be blameless before Yahweh your God.

lines.text: The same word: you shall be tamim before the Lord. Is the Bible setting us up for failure? No. Tamim means blameless, but also complete, mature, even innocent.
It comes right before the promise of 'a prophet like me' (Deuteronomy 18:15) whom Israel must listen to. The Greek Old Testament translates tamim here with teleios, the word Matthew uses in 5:48.

src.text: He who walks blamelessly, and works righteousness, / And speaks truth in his heart.

lines.text: The word of God expects you to be tamim. And the psalm ends: 'He who does these things will never be shaken.'
God said to Abram, 'Walk before Me and be blameless' (Genesis 17:1); Noah was 'blameless among those in his generations' (Genesis 6:9). Neither was flawless; both walked with God.

left.text: Be merciful, just as your Father is merciful.

right.text: Therefore you are to be perfect, as your heavenly Father is perfect.

lines.text: This is the context of 5:48: be tamim, mature in the way you show your love, a love that reaches even the most difficult people in your circles of influence.
The 'therefore' ties 5:48 to the sun and rain of 5:45. Luke's parallel puts the same idea as mercy.

FAMILY.title: Sons do what the Father does

left.text: Truly, truly, I say to you, the Son can do nothing from Himself, unless it is something He sees the Father doing; for whatever the Father does, these things the Son also does in the same manner.

right.text: so that you may be sons of your Father who is in heaven; for He causes His sun to rise on the evil and the good, and sends rain on the righteous and the unrighteous.

lines.text: In the Jewish mindset, the family business is the sons furthering the father's work. For Jesus, that business is spreading the kingdom of God on earth, and kingdom love reaches everyone, enemies included.
'Sons of God' already appeared in the Beatitudes: 'Blessed are the peacemakers, for they shall be called sons of God' (5:9).

FAMILY.title: He shows love for the sojourner

src.text: He executes justice for the orphan and the widow, and shows love for the sojourner by giving him food and clothing. So show love for the sojourner, for you were sojourners in the land of Egypt.

lines.text: The people had forgotten that they were once outcasts themselves, slaves in Egypt, and God's clear teaching to care for the outcast, which extends to Gentiles too, some of them in this very crowd. See also Psalm 146, Zechariah 7 and Malachi 3.

src.text: Moreover, I will give you a new heart and put a new spirit within you; and I will remove the heart of stone from your flesh and give you a heart of flesh.

lines.text: All of this is impossible without the Holy Spirit, replacing our hearts of stone with hearts of flesh. And some enemies, loved this way, will be transformed and adopted into God's family.
'We love, because He first loved us' (1 John 4:19).

PEOPLE.name: Jesus
PEOPLE.video: As the new Moses, gives commands that are 'nothing new': He re-teaches the Torah from the heart.
PEOPLE.bg: 'But I say to you' six times: Jesus speaks on His own authority, which is why the crowds were astonished (7:28-29).

PEOPLE.name: The ancients
PEOPLE.video: 'You have heard that the ancients were told': the generation that received the Law, and the teaching passed down since.
PEOPLE.bg: The LSB's 'ancients' (5:21, 33) translates archaioi, 'those of old.'

PEOPLE.name: The scribes and Pharisees
PEOPLE.video: The backdrop of every saying: the model of righteousness Jesus' disciples must surpass (5:20).
PEOPLE.bg: Matthew 23 later shows their oath rules (23:16-22) and their care for small tithes while neglecting 'justice and mercy and faithfulness' (23:23).

PEOPLE.name: Tax collectors and Gentiles
PEOPLE.video: Jesus' examples of people who love only those who love them back (5:46-47), people some in the crowd despised.
PEOPLE.bg: Tax collectors worked for Rome or for Herod Antipas and were seen as collaborators. Matthew himself was one (9:9).

PEOPLE.name: The sojourner, the orphan and the widow
PEOPLE.video: The outcasts God loves and Israel had forgotten (Deuteronomy 10; Psalm 146; Zechariah 7; Malachi 3).
PEOPLE.bg: The Law repeatedly ties care for them to Israel's own story: 'you were sojourners in the land of Egypt' (Deuteronomy 10:19).

PEOPLE.name: Moses
PEOPLE.video: Jesus is the new Moses, interpreting what was given 'from the very beginning.'
PEOPLE.bg: Moses gave the commands Jesus quotes (Exodus 20-21; Leviticus 19; Deuteronomy 24).

TERMS.term: You have heard... but I say to you
TERMS.def: The six sayings of 5:21-48, often called the antitheses. The video stresses they are not new law but the heart of the old.
An Aramaic insult, roughly 'empty-head.' Chrysostom says it shows 'some contempt and slight on the part of the speaker' (Homilies on Matthew 16).
The council: Jerusalem's highest Jewish court (LSB 5:22). Local courts sat in the towns.
From the valley of the son of Hinnom outside Jerusalem (Jeremiah 7:31-32), a picture of final judgment. The video links it to Isaiah 66.
A small Roman copper coin, a quarter of an as (5:26): 'the last penny.'
The written release in Deuteronomy 24:1 that let a divorced woman remarry.
'Forces' (angareuō) is a Persian loanword for compelled service: a soldier could make a civilian carry his pack. Jesus says go two.
A rabbinic idea (Mishnah, Avot 1:1): extra rules that keep you far from breaking a command. Jesus' fence is around the heart.
Hebrew: blameless, whole, complete, mature (H8549). The video's key to 'perfect' in 5:48.
The tradition of interpretation that the rabbis held was passed down alongside the written Law; later written in the Mishnah (c. AD 200) and Talmud. The video sees Jesus correcting it in this sermon.

WORDS.gloss: To be angry. The heart-root of murder.
Raca: an Aramaic term of contempt, 'empty one.'
Foolish, stupid (our 'moron'). Same root as the verb for salt that has 'become tasteless' (5:13).
Gehenna, from Hebrew gē hinnōm, the valley of Hinnom. LSB 'hell.' Look up: BDAG, γέεννα.
To desire, long for; here, to lust. The Greek Old Testament uses it in the commandment 'You shall not covet' (Exodus 20:17).
A certificate of divorce, a written release.
Sexual immorality: the one exception in 5:32. Look up: BDAG, πορνεία.
To press into service, compel (LSB 'forces'), from the Persian royal courier system.
To love: chosen, active good will, here aimed at enemies.
Complete, mature, perfect; having reached its goal (telos). Look up: BDAG, τέλειος.
Complete, whole, blameless, sound; used of unblemished sacrifices and of people who walk with God. Look up: BDB or HALOT, תָּמִים.
To love: 'you shall love your neighbor as yourself.'
Hinnom, the valley south of Jerusalem: the source of the word Gehenna.

BACKGROUND.p: Towns had local courts of elders; Jerusalem's Sanhedrin was the high council. 'Make friends quickly with your opponent at law' (5:25) reflects how a dispute could end in debtors' prison.

Jewish teachers argued over the 'indecency' of Deuteronomy 24:1. The Mishnah (Gittin 9:10) records the school of Shammai allowing divorce only for unchastity and the school of Hillel for almost any reason. Jesus' answer is closest to the strict view.
People swore 'by heaven' or 'by Jerusalem' to sound serious while avoiding God's name. Jesus says all of these still belong to God (5:34-36), so simply tell the truth.
Soldiers could legally compel civilians to carry loads for a set distance. A Roman mile was about 1,480 m (1,000 paces).

The Mishnah collects rabbinic teaching written down around AD 200; the Talmuds add later discussion (the Babylonian Talmud around AD 500). They help show how Jews read the Law, but they are later than the Gospels, so dates matter.

WITNESSES.text: Do you see authority in perfection? Do you see a bearing suited to a legislator? Why, which among prophets ever spoke on this wise?
WITNESSES.src: Homilies on Matthew 16, on 'But I say to you' (5:22). Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, series 1, vol. 10 (public domain).

WITNESSES.text: Do you see how many steps He has ascended, and how He has set us on the very summit of virtue?
WITNESSES.src: Homilies on Matthew 18, on loving enemies (5:43-48). Same source.

DEBATES.h: Is Jesus correcting the Law or its interpreters?
DEBATES.p: The video: Jesus re-teaches the Torah and corrects the oral tradition, not the Law itself. Others note that some sayings ('make no oath at all,' 'do not resist') go beyond what the Law required, so Jesus is fulfilling the Law by taking it further. Both agree Jesus does not set the Law aside (5:17).
Whole and mature (tamim), as the video says; or complete in love, from the context of 5:43-47; or the final goal believers grow toward. Most hold these together.

Some read it as a call to absolute non-violence; others as personal non-retaliation that does not forbid just courts or protection of others (compare Romans 12:19-13:4). All agree it rules out revenge.
What 'sexual immorality' (porneia) covers in 5:32 and 19:9, and whether remarriage is allowed after a permitted divorce, are long-debated.

CAREFUL_INTRO: Small slips worth knowing (offered gently; the video's main points stand):
CAREFUL: 'You shall not murder' is Exodus 20:13; the captions say 'Exodus 20:3.'

Deuteronomy 24:1-4 regulates divorce rather than saying 'avoid divorce at all costs.' Malachi 2:16 ('For I hate divorce') is closer to that point, and Jesus explains Moses' permission in Matthew 19:8.
The Talmud was compiled about AD 500, so its saying about public humiliation is later than Jesus (though quoted as an older teaching). The comparison still shows how deep Jesus goes.
'Hate your enemy' is not in the Law. Leviticus 19:18 limits 'neighbor' to 'the sons of your people,' but Leviticus 19:34 extends that love to the sojourner. The video's point about tribalism stands.
The video says Jesus went up the mountain 'by verse 24 of chapter 4'; the crowds gather in 4:24-25, and He goes up in 5:1.

Matthew wrote in Greek: 'perfect' is teleios. The link to tamim is real (the Greek Old Testament uses teleios for tamim in Deuteronomy 18:13), but the Hebrew word is the background, not Matthew's own word.

QUESTIONS: Before this video, how did you hear 'you are to be perfect'? How does tamim (whole, mature, blameless) change it?
Pick one of the six sayings. What is the outward command, and what heart issue does Jesus put His 'fence' around?
Jesus puts reconciliation before worship (5:23-24). Is there someone you need to make peace with before you next come to worship?
Who is the 'enemy' or outsider in your circles of influence? What would loving and praying for them look like this week?
The video says sons do what the Father does. Where do you see God's 'sun and rain' kindness in your life that you could pass on?
Our society is 'divided, tribal, territorial and adversarial.' How can Christians model 5:43-48 online?
APPLICATION_VIDEO: The lesson for the original audience: God loves His enemies, so in God's kingdom we should be like God and love our enemies. Simple, but incredibly challenging. The lesson is the same today, in a society that has become so divided, tribal, territorial and adversarial: will you love your enemies? Will you be tamim the way your heavenly Father is tamim? If you will, you will be sons and daughters of your Father in heaven. This is impossible without the Holy Spirit replacing our hearts of stone with hearts of flesh.
APPLICATION_ADDED: Study note (added): Jesus gives a first step that anyone can take: 'pray for those who persecute you' (5:44). Write down one name this week and pray for that person's good every day. Then look for one concrete kindness, like returning an enemy's stray ox (Exodus 23:4).

# Matthew 5:21-48 Study Notes: The Most IMPOSSIBLE Verse in the Gospels?! (Matthew 5:21-48)
Video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=jwxj10dmCA4
Channel: Every Word | Length: 24:25 | Series: The Gospel of Matthew Every Word (playlist of 58 videos)
Series hub: https://shea-nelson.github.io/workout-app/bible/
Study page: https://shea-nelson.github.io/workout-app/bible/matthew-7/
PDF for Goodnotes: https://shea-nelson.github.io/workout-app/bible/assets/Matthew-Ep07-Be-Whole-Like-Your-Father.pdf
Translation: Legacy Standard Bible (LSB). The video reads from another English translation; quotations here are LSB. Notes marked [Background] are added study helps, not from the video.

## Summary (from the video)
- The teacher reads Matthew 5:21-48: six times Jesus says 'You have heard... but I say to you,' on anger, lust, divorce, oaths, retaliation and love for enemies, ending with 'you are to be perfect, as your heavenly Father is perfect' (5:48).
- The thread is personal relationships: anger with a brother, an opponent at law, lust, divorce, oaths, generosity, loving everyone. Our relationships are how we bring God's kingdom on earth.
- These are not new commands. As the new Moses, Jesus re-teaches the Torah from the heart, against the backdrop of the scribes and Pharisees (5:20).
- Jesus puts a 'fence around the Torah,' a rabbinic way of teaching, but His fence is around the heart, where sin begins. The Talmud compares public humiliation to shedding blood; Jesus goes deeper, to anger.
- 'Perfect' echoes the Hebrew tamim: blameless, whole, mature (2 Samuel 22:31; Deuteronomy 18:13; Psalm 15:2). The Bible is looking for maturity, not flawlessness.
- The lesson: God loves His enemies, sending sun and rain on the evil and the good, so in His kingdom we love our enemies too. Sons do what the Father does (John 5:19). Will you be tamim as your heavenly Father is tamim?

## Key quotes from the video (auto-captions, lightly cleaned)
> "When Jesus said that you must be perfect as your heavenly Father is perfect, He wasn't intending to make you anxious or fearful."
> "The fence that Jesus is placing forces His people to deal with what is on the inside, what is in their heart, which is where sin originates."
> "The Bible is not looking for flawlessness; it's looking for maturity."
> "God loves His enemies; therefore in God's kingdom we should be like God and love our enemies."
> "Will you love your enemies? Will you be tamim the way your heavenly Father is tamim?"

### Read the six sayings in pairs
Each saying has two halves: 'You have heard' (what the Law said) and 'But I say to you' (where Jesus takes it). Look up each Old Testament text first, then ask the video's question: is Jesus replacing the Torah, or showing its heart?

## Scripture passages covered

## You have heard... but I say to you
1. 1 · Matthew 5:21-26: Murder and anger
   You have heard (Exodus 20:13, LSB): "You shall not murder."
   But I say to you (Matthew 5:22, LSB): "But I say to you that everyone who is angry with his brother shall be guilty before the court; and whoever says to his brother, ‘Raca,’ shall be guilty before the Sanhedrin; and whoever says, ‘You fool,’ shall be guilty enough to go into the fiery hell."
   (video) If you bear anger in your heart, you're already on the path toward murder, because murder usually begins in anger.
   [Background] Then two practical scenes: leave your offering at the altar and 'first be reconciled to your brother' (5:24), and make friends quickly with your opponent at law (5:25). Reconciliation comes before worship. (Matthew 5:23-26)
   Chrysostom: 'Do you see authority in perfection? ... Which among prophets ever spoke on this wise? ... None; but, Thus says the Lord' (Homilies on Matthew 16).
2. 2 · Matthew 5:27-30: Adultery and the heart
   You have heard (Exodus 20:14, LSB): "You shall not commit adultery."
   But I say to you (Matthew 5:28, LSB): "but I say to you that everyone who looks at a woman to lust for her has already committed adultery with her in his heart."
   (video) The shift is from actions performed in front of others to what only God sees, the heart.
   [Background] The tenth commandment already reached the heart: 'You shall not covet your neighbor's wife' (Exodus 20:17). Tearing out an eye and cutting off a hand (5:29-30) is a vivid way of saying: deal ruthlessly with what leads you to sin. (Exodus 20:17; Matthew 5:29-30)
3. 3 · Matthew 5:31-32: Divorce
   It was said (Deuteronomy 24:1, LSB): "and he writes her a certificate of divorce and puts it in her hand and sends her out from his house,"
   But I say to you (Matthew 5:32, LSB): "but I say to you that everyone who divorces his wife, except for the reason of sexual immorality, makes her commit adultery; and whoever marries a divorced woman commits adultery."
   (video) Avoid divorce: the video points to Deuteronomy 24:1 and Jeremiah 3:1. (Jeremiah 3:1)
   [Background] Deuteronomy 24 regulates divorce rather than commands it. Later Jesus explains: 'Because of your hardness of heart Moses permitted you to divorce your wives; but from the beginning it has not been this way' (Matthew 19:8). Compare Malachi 2:16. (Matthew 19:3-9; Malachi 2:14-16)
4. 4 · Matthew 5:33-37: Oaths
   You have heard (Leviticus 19:12, LSB): "And you shall not swear falsely by My name, so as to profane the name of your God; I am Yahweh."
   But I say to you (Matthew 5:34, LSB): "But I say to you, make no oath at all, either by heaven, for it is the throne of God,"
   (video) The video lists Leviticus 19:12 and Numbers 30:2 behind this saying. (Numbers 30:2)
   [Background] 'Let your statement be, ‘Yes, yes’ or ‘No, no’' (5:37). If your word is always true, you don't need an oath to prop it up. Jesus later exposes clever oath rules in Matthew 23:16-22. (Matthew 5:37; Matthew 23:16-22; James 5:12)
5. 5 · Matthew 5:38-42: An eye for an eye
   You have heard (Exodus 21:24, LSB): "eye for eye, tooth for tooth, hand for hand, foot for foot,"
   But I say to you (Matthew 5:39, LSB): "But I say to you, do not resist an evil person; but whoever slaps you on your right cheek, turn the other to him also."
   (video) Forgiving others and being radically generous.
   [Background] In the Law, 'eye for eye' guided judges and limited revenge to fit the harm (Exodus 21:23-25; Leviticus 24:20; Deuteronomy 19:21). Leviticus 19:18 already said, 'You shall not take vengeance.' Jesus asks for more than restraint: turn the cheek, give the garment, go the second mile. (Leviticus 24:19-20; Deuteronomy 19:21; Leviticus 19:18)
   Chrysostom on 5:39-41: 'Do you see the height of self-denial?' (Homilies on Matthew 18).
6. 6 · Matthew 5:43-48: Love your enemies
   You have heard (Leviticus 19:18, LSB): "You shall not take vengeance, and you shall not keep your anger against the sons of your people, but you shall love your neighbor as yourself; I am Yahweh."
   But I say to you (Matthew 5:44-45, LSB): "But I say to you, love your enemies and pray for those who persecute you, so that you may be sons of your Father who is in heaven"
   (video) The video's focus. Jewish sentiment had become tribal: love of neighbor reached only 'the sons of your people' (Leviticus 19:18). They had forgotten that God is for the outcast, the sojourner, the orphan and the widow.
   [Background] 'Hate your enemy' is not a command in the Law. The same chapter says of the sojourner, 'you shall love him as yourself' (Leviticus 19:34), and Exodus tells Israel to return an enemy's stray ox (Exodus 23:4-5). (Leviticus 19:33-34; Exodus 23:4-5; Proverbs 25:21)
   Chrysostom on this last step: 'Do you see how many steps He has ascended, and how He has set us on the very summit of virtue?' (Homilies on Matthew 18).

## A fence around the heart
1. A rabbinic way of teaching: A fence around the Torah
   Mishnah, Avot 1:1: "make a fence round the Torah"
   (video) Imagine sin as a place on a map. A fence keeps you far from it. Other rabbis did this, but Jesus' fence is not more outward rules that can be performed for others to see; it is around the heart.
   [Background] This saying is credited to the Men of the Great Assembly at the start of the Mishnah's tractate Avot ('Fathers'), written down around AD 200. Translation: Joshua Kulp, Mishnah Yomit (CC BY), via Sefaria.
2. Anger or humiliation?: Deeper than public shame
   Babylonian Talmud, Bava Metzia 58b: "Anyone who humiliates another in public, it is as though he were spilling blood."
   (video) The Talmud, the written account of the oral Torah, says this. Jesus goes further back, to anger in the heart. Public humiliation doesn't go deep enough; it doesn't track back to the source.
   [Debated] The Talmud was compiled centuries after Jesus (around AD 500). This saying is quoted there as an older teaching, so it may reflect earlier rabbis, but we cannot be sure it was taught in Jesus' day. Translation: William Davidson edition (CC BY-NC), via Sefaria.
3. The fiery hell · Matthew 5:22, 29-30: Isaiah's unquenched fire
   Isaiah (Isaiah 66:24, LSB): "Then they will go forth and look / On the corpses of the men / Who have transgressed against Me. / For their worm will not die / And their fire will not be quenched;"
   Jesus (Mark 9:47-48, LSB): "it is better for you to enter the kingdom of God with one eye, than, having two eyes, to be cast into hell, where their worm does not die, and the fire is not quenched."
   (video) When Jesus speaks of hell or the judgment of fire (5:22, 29), He is drawing on Isaiah 66:15 to the end of the chapter. Read Isaiah 66 alongside Matthew 5:22-30. (Isaiah 66:15-16)
   [Background] Mark's version of the eye saying quotes Isaiah 66:24 outright. 'Hell' is Gehenna, the valley of the son of Hinnom outside Jerusalem, where children had been burned to idols (Jeremiah 7:31-32). (Jeremiah 7:31-32)

## Perfect means tamim
"Therefore you are to be perfect, as your heavenly Father is perfect." (Matthew 5:48, LSB)
1. God is tamim: His way is blameless
   Tamim 2 Samuel 22:31: "As for God, His way is blameless; / The word of Yahweh is tried; / He is a shield to all who take refuge in Him." https://read.lsbible.org/?q=2+Samuel+22:31
   (video) The Hebrew word here is tamim: blameless. And Jesus says, be like this.
2. The closest parallel to 5:48: You shall be blameless
   Tamim Deuteronomy 18:13: "You shall be blameless before Yahweh your God." https://read.lsbible.org/?q=Deuteronomy+18:13
   (video) The same word: you shall be tamim before the Lord. Is the Bible setting us up for failure? No. Tamim means blameless, but also complete, mature, even innocent.
   [Background] It comes right before the promise of 'a prophet like me' (Deuteronomy 18:15) whom Israel must listen to. The Greek Old Testament translates tamim here with teleios, the word Matthew uses in 5:48. (Deuteronomy 18:13-15)
3. Walk it out: He who walks blamelessly
   Tamim Psalm 15:2: "He who walks blamelessly, and works righteousness, / And speaks truth in his heart." https://read.lsbible.org/?q=Psalm+15:2
   (video) The word of God expects you to be tamim. And the psalm ends: 'He who does these things will never be shaken.'
   [Background] God said to Abram, 'Walk before Me and be blameless' (Genesis 17:1); Noah was 'blameless among those in his generations' (Genesis 6:9). Neither was flawless; both walked with God. (Genesis 17:1; Genesis 6:9; Psalm 15:5)
4. In context · Matthew 5:45-48: Perfect in love
   Luke's version (Luke 6:36, LSB): "Be merciful, just as your Father is merciful."
   Matthew (Matthew 5:48, LSB): "Therefore you are to be perfect, as your heavenly Father is perfect."
   (video) This is the context of 5:48: be tamim, mature in the way you show your love, a love that reaches even the most difficult people in your circles of influence.
   [Background] The 'therefore' ties 5:48 to the sun and rain of 5:45. Luke's parallel puts the same idea as mercy. (Luke 6:35-36)

## Sons do what the Father does
1. The family business · Matthew 5:45: Sons do what the Father does
   Jesus in John (John 5:19, LSB): "Truly, truly, I say to you, the Son can do nothing from Himself, unless it is something He sees the Father doing; for whatever the Father does, these things the Son also does in the same manner."
   Jesus in Matthew (Matthew 5:45, LSB): "so that you may be sons of your Father who is in heaven; for He causes His sun to rise on the evil and the good, and sends rain on the righteous and the unrighteous."
   (video) In the Jewish mindset, the family business is the sons furthering the father's work. For Jesus, that business is spreading the kingdom of God on earth, and kingdom love reaches everyone, enemies included.
   [Background] 'Sons of God' already appeared in the Beatitudes: 'Blessed are the peacemakers, for they shall be called sons of God' (5:9). (Matthew 5:9)
2. God is for the outcast: He shows love for the sojourner
   Remember Deuteronomy 10:18-19: "He executes justice for the orphan and the widow, and shows love for the sojourner by giving him food and clothing. So show love for the sojourner, for you were sojourners in the land of Egypt." https://read.lsbible.org/?q=Deuteronomy+10:18-19
   (video) The people had forgotten that they were once outcasts themselves, slaves in Egypt, and God's clear teaching to care for the outcast, which extends to Gentiles too, some of them in this very crowd. See also Psalm 146, Zechariah 7 and Malachi 3. (Psalm 146:9; Zechariah 7:9-10; Malachi 3:5)
3. Only by the Spirit: A heart of flesh
   Promise Ezekiel 36:26: "Moreover, I will give you a new heart and put a new spirit within you; and I will remove the heart of stone from your flesh and give you a heart of flesh." https://read.lsbible.org/?q=Ezekiel+36:26
   (video) All of this is impossible without the Holy Spirit, replacing our hearts of stone with hearts of flesh. And some enemies, loved this way, will be transformed and adopted into God's family.
   [Background] 'We love, because He first loved us' (1 John 4:19). (1 John 4:19)

## Key people
- Jesus: As the new Moses, gives commands that are 'nothing new': He re-teaches the Torah from the heart. [Background] 'But I say to you' six times: Jesus speaks on His own authority, which is why the crowds were astonished (7:28-29).
- The ancients: 'You have heard that the ancients were told': the generation that received the Law, and the teaching passed down since. [Background] The LSB's 'ancients' (5:21, 33) translates archaioi, 'those of old.'
- The scribes and Pharisees: The backdrop of every saying: the model of righteousness Jesus' disciples must surpass (5:20). [Background] Matthew 23 later shows their oath rules (23:16-22) and their care for small tithes while neglecting 'justice and mercy and faithfulness' (23:23).
- Tax collectors and Gentiles: Jesus' examples of people who love only those who love them back (5:46-47), people some in the crowd despised. [Background] Tax collectors worked for Rome or for Herod Antipas and were seen as collaborators. Matthew himself was one (9:9).
- The sojourner, the orphan and the widow: The outcasts God loves and Israel had forgotten (Deuteronomy 10; Psalm 146; Zechariah 7; Malachi 3). [Background] The Law repeatedly ties care for them to Israel's own story: 'you were sojourners in the land of Egypt' (Deuteronomy 10:19).
- Moses: Jesus is the new Moses, interpreting what was given 'from the very beginning.' [Background] Moses gave the commands Jesus quotes (Exodus 20-21; Leviticus 19; Deuteronomy 24).

## Places [Background]
- Mount of Beatitudes: The traditional site of the sermon, above Tabgha.
- Capernaum: Jesus' home base by the lake (4:13).
- Tiberias: Herod Antipas' new capital, founded around AD 20, seat of his court.
- Magdala: A busy fishing town on the west shore.
- Hippos: A Gentile Decapolis city across the lake: the kind of neighbors 5:47 has in mind.
- Bethsaida: Home town of Andrew and Peter (John 1:44).
- Nazareth: Jesus' hometown.

## Key terms
- You have heard... but I say to you: The six sayings of 5:21-48, often called the antitheses. The video stresses they are not new law but the heart of the old.
- Raca: An Aramaic insult, roughly 'empty-head.' Chrysostom says it shows 'some contempt and slight on the part of the speaker' (Homilies on Matthew 16). [Background]
- Sanhedrin: The council: Jerusalem's highest Jewish court (LSB 5:22). Local courts sat in the towns. [Background]
- Fiery hell (Gehenna): From the valley of the son of Hinnom outside Jerusalem (Jeremiah 7:31-32), a picture of final judgment. The video links it to Isaiah 66.
- Quadrans: A small Roman copper coin, a quarter of an as (5:26): 'the last penny.' [Background]
- Certificate of divorce: The written release in Deuteronomy 24:1 that let a divorced woman remarry. [Background]
- Go one mile: 'Forces' (angareuō) is a Persian loanword for compelled service: a soldier could make a civilian carry his pack. Jesus says go two. [Background]
- Fence around the Torah: A rabbinic idea (Mishnah, Avot 1:1): extra rules that keep you far from breaking a command. Jesus' fence is around the heart.
- Tamim: Hebrew: blameless, whole, complete, mature (H8549). The video's key to 'perfect' in 5:48.
- Oral Torah: The tradition of interpretation that the rabbis held was passed down alongside the written Law; later written in the Mishnah (c. AD 200) and Talmud. The video sees Jesus correcting it in this sermon.

## Historical and cultural background [Background: established]
- Courts in Jesus' day: Towns had local courts of elders; Jerusalem's Sanhedrin was the high council. 'Make friends quickly with your opponent at law' (5:25) reflects how a dispute could end in debtors' prison.
- Divorce debates: Jewish teachers argued over the 'indecency' of Deuteronomy 24:1. The Mishnah (Gittin 9:10) records the school of Shammai allowing divorce only for unchastity and the school of Hillel for almost any reason. Jesus' answer is closest to the strict view.
- Oaths: People swore 'by heaven' or 'by Jerusalem' to sound serious while avoiding God's name. Jesus says all of these still belong to God (5:34-36), so simply tell the truth.
- Roman occupation: Soldiers could legally compel civilians to carry loads for a set distance. A Roman mile was about 1,480 m (1,000 paces).
- The Mishnah and Talmud: The Mishnah collects rabbinic teaching written down around AD 200; the Talmuds add later discussion (the Babylonian Talmud around AD 500). They help show how Jews read the Law, but they are later than the Gospels, so dates matter.

## Early witnesses [Background: sourced]
- John Chrysostom (c. AD 390): "Do you see authority in perfection? Do you see a bearing suited to a legislator? Why, which among prophets ever spoke on this wise?" Homilies on Matthew 16, on 'But I say to you' (5:22). Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, series 1, vol. 10 (public domain).
- John Chrysostom (c. AD 390): "Do you see how many steps He has ascended, and how He has set us on the very summit of virtue?" Homilies on Matthew 18, on loving enemies (5:43-48). Same source.

## Where scholars differ [Background: debated]
- Is Jesus correcting the Law or its interpreters? The video: Jesus re-teaches the Torah and corrects the oral tradition, not the Law itself. Others note that some sayings ('make no oath at all,' 'do not resist') go beyond what the Law required, so Jesus is fulfilling the Law by taking it further. Both agree Jesus does not set the Law aside (5:17).
- What does 'perfect' mean? Whole and mature (tamim), as the video says; or complete in love, from the context of 5:43-47; or the final goal believers grow toward. Most hold these together.
- Turn the other cheek Some read it as a call to absolute non-violence; others as personal non-retaliation that does not forbid just courts or protection of others (compare Romans 12:19-13:4). All agree it rules out revenge.
- The exception clause What 'sexual immorality' (porneia) covers in 5:32 and 19:9, and whether remarriage is allowed after a permitted divorce, are long-debated.

## Careful reading notes
Small slips worth knowing (offered gently; the video's main points stand):
- 'You shall not murder' is Exodus 20:13; the captions say 'Exodus 20:3.'
- Deuteronomy 24:1-4 regulates divorce rather than saying 'avoid divorce at all costs.' Malachi 2:16 ('For I hate divorce') is closer to that point, and Jesus explains Moses' permission in Matthew 19:8.
- The Talmud was compiled about AD 500, so its saying about public humiliation is later than Jesus (though quoted as an older teaching). The comparison still shows how deep Jesus goes.
- 'Hate your enemy' is not in the Law. Leviticus 19:18 limits 'neighbor' to 'the sons of your people,' but Leviticus 19:34 extends that love to the sojourner. The video's point about tribalism stands.
- The video says Jesus went up the mountain 'by verse 24 of chapter 4'; the crowds gather in 4:24-25, and He goes up in 5:1.
- Matthew wrote in Greek: 'perfect' is teleios. The link to tamim is real (the Greek Old Testament uses teleios for tamim in Deuteronomy 18:13), but the Hebrew word is the background, not Matthew's own word.

## Reflection and discussion questions
1. Before this video, how did you hear 'you are to be perfect'? How does tamim (whole, mature, blameless) change it?
2. Pick one of the six sayings. What is the outward command, and what heart issue does Jesus put His 'fence' around?
3. Jesus puts reconciliation before worship (5:23-24). Is there someone you need to make peace with before you next come to worship?
4. Who is the 'enemy' or outsider in your circles of influence? What would loving and praying for them look like this week?
5. The video says sons do what the Father does. Where do you see God's 'sun and rain' kindness in your life that you could pass on?
6. Our society is 'divided, tribal, territorial and adversarial.' How can Christians model 5:43-48 online?

## Application
- (video) The lesson for the original audience: God loves His enemies, so in God's kingdom we should be like God and love our enemies. Simple, but incredibly challenging. The lesson is the same today, in a society that has become so divided, tribal, territorial and adversarial: will you love your enemies? Will you be tamim the way your heavenly Father is tamim? If you will, you will be sons and daughters of your Father in heaven. This is impossible without the Holy Spirit replacing our hearts of stone with hearts of flesh.
- Study note (added): Jesus gives a first step that anyone can take: 'pray for those who persecute you' (5:44). Write down one name this week and pray for that person's good every day. Then look for one concrete kindness, like returning an enemy's stray ox (Exodus 23:4).
